question: Move the AED at P.S. 197 John B. Russwurm into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 197 John B. Russwurm (School, ZIP 10037) has a registered AED at "outside main office; Basement, Outside Gym".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.28 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 4 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 3 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY EMS Station 16, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 103 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving the AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap in coverage. The school's current indoor placement is reachable only 55 of 168 hours during the school year [E3], and the area experienced 1.28 cardiac-arrest calls annually during hours when no nearby AED was accessible [E4]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED is associated with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. While the fire station 103 meters away could be an alternative [E8], a street-wall cabinet would ensure immediate public access without depending on station staffing. This modest intervention could meaningfully improve survival odds for residents in this high-need zone.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate presents a compelling gap, but the case for this specific move remains uncertain. Yes, the school's current location is inaccessible 113 hours weekly during the school year [E3], and 1.28 calls annually occurred during coverage gaps [E4]. However, we don't know the actual street locations of those calls—they're only ZIP-coded [E9]—so we can't confirm they'd reach a street-wall cabinet. The fire station 103 meters away [E8] is a serious alternative that deserves exploration first: it's staffed around the clock and requires no new infrastructure. We also lack critical information: cabinet cost, vandalism risk at this location, and whether the school already permits after-hours access [E9]. Before committing resources, we should verify the fire station's feasibility and clarify whether those 1.28 calls would actually benefit from street-wall placement rather than FDNY coordination.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that we lack street-level call locations [E9], so we cannot guarantee every call would reach a street-wall cabinet. However, the fire station alternative has a critical gap: those 1.28 annual calls occurred during hours when every nearby AED was shut [E4], which suggests FDNY coordination alone has not solved the access problem. The fire station is 103 meters away [E8], but distance and staffing availability are different things—we don't know if station protocols currently prioritize rapid AED retrieval for public use. A street-wall cabinet removes that dependency entirely. Given that bystander shock with public AEDs reaches 66.5% survival [E7], the modest risk of exploring this option seems justified before defaulting to an untested institutional arrangement.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate makes a fair point that FDNY coordination hasn't eliminated the 1.28 annual calls during coverage gaps [E4], and that institutional arrangements carry uncertainty. But that's precisely why we should test the fire station option first before installing new infrastructure. We don't know whether those calls occurred near the fire station or elsewhere in the ZIP [E9], so we can't assume a street-wall cabinet would reach them either. The fire station is only 103 meters away [E8]—well within two-minute walking distance—and staffed around the clock. A conversation with FDNY about rapid public AED access there costs nothing and might solve the problem without cabinet expenses, vandalism risk, or maintenance burden [E9]. If that fails, the street-wall cabinet becomes a stronger case.

verdict.summary: Strong evidence of coverage gap (1.28 annual calls during AED-unavailable hours) and survival benefit of public AEDs (66.5% vs 43.0%). However, ZIP-level call data prevents confirmation that street-wall placement would reach those calls. Fire station alternative 103m away warrants exploration first.
verdict.strongestFor: 1.28 annual calls occur when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]; public AED shock associates with 66.5% survival [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Actual call locations unknown—only ZIP-coded [E9]. Fire station 103m away staffed 24/7 [E8] offers untested alternative requiring no new infrastructure.
verdict.nextStep: Contact FDNY Station 16 to assess feasibility and timeline for 24/7 public AED access before committing to cabinet installation.
